**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Reconstruct the outline behind somebody else's paper. Build your own the same way, topic sentence by topic sentence. Then defend your research problem in front of the room.

## Before class

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

Academic writing I — the method. A paper is built outline first. One topic sentence per paragraph, in order, before any prose exists. We start backwards. Take a published paper apart into the outline that must have produced it. That is also this week's exercise, and the fastest way to see that good writing has a skeleton. Then forwards: outline, sketch, full text. Every written product in this course is submitted in those stages, so the argument is fixed before the sentences are. Then what a problem statement in particular has to do. Scope, unit, population. The 'so what' in the first sentence, not the fourth paragraph. And the failure modes: the topic with no question, hedging, the buried claim, the review that reviews without arguing.

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

Each team presents its research problem in five minutes. The presentation is this morning's method under test, because your five slides are an outline. One topic sentence per slide. No bullet lists. If the argument does not stand up as five sentences, it will not stand up at five pages, and the room will see which it is. Questions are aimed at the skeleton: where does the argument jump? Then you rate your teammates for the first time.

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.

## Due

Present your research problem, in class · Rate your teammates
